---
title: "Intravenous Phosphate and 28-Day Mortality in ICU Hypophosphatemia: A Sequential Target Trial Emulation"
---


## Abstract

**Background**: Hypophosphatemia affects approximately one in four critically ill patients and has been associated with adverse outcomes, including prolonged mechanical ventilation and increased mortality. Whether intravenous phosphate supplementation reduces mortality remains uncertain. Observational studies have yielded contradictory findings, and no adequately powered randomized trials are available. Prior evidence has been compromised by immortal time bias, confounding by indication, and inconsistent adjustment strategies.

**Methods**: We conducted a sequential target trial emulation using the SEQTaRget cloning-censoring-weighting framework in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV v3.1, 2008–2022). Adults with an ICU stay of ≥24 hours and serum phosphate ≤0.80 mmol/L contributed 32,330 sequential trial-periods. The primary estimand was the 28-day restricted mean survival time (RMST) difference, which does not rely on the proportional hazards assumption. The complementary estimand was the overall 28-day mortality HR via SEQTaRget ITT (14 DAG-specified covariates, Rubin's rules across 20 multiply imputed datasets, 200 bootstrap iterations). The ITT HR is reported as a time-averaged effect because the proportional hazards assumption was strongly violated. Piecewise HRs across pre-specified intervals (0–3, 3–7, 7–14, 14–28 days) were designated as complementary estimands.

**Results**: Under the proportional hazards violation, the time-averaged ITT HR was 0.987 (95% CI, 0.893–1.092; p=0.802) and the 28-day RMST difference was −0.02 days (95% CI, −0.31 to 0.27; p=0.880), together establishing no net survival benefit. Daily-resolution analysis revealed temporal heterogeneity: a protective signal on Day 1 (HR=0.565; 95% CI, 0.401–0.796; nominal p=0.001; not corrected for multiplicity) was followed by elevated risk during Days 5–8 (HR range 1.47–1.59, all p<0.005), with the 3–7 day interval reaching significance (HR=1.308; 95% CI, 1.154–1.484; p<0.001). No interaction test reached FDR significance (all q>0.10), although the Charlson comorbidity index showed a nominal interaction (p=0.013, q=0.134). A post-hoc phosphate threshold dose-response analysis revealed a monotonic protective pattern: IV phosphate significantly reduced 28-day mortality only in patients with baseline phosphate <0.50 mmol/L (HR=0.806; 95% CI, 0.670–0.970; p=0.022; n=2,852), with the effect attenuating progressively toward the null at higher thresholds (HR=0.92–0.97 at 0.60–0.80 mmol/L). All sensitivity analyses, including the per-protocol analysis (HR=0.979; 95% CI, 0.885–1.083), were consistent with the overall null finding.

**Conclusions**: The overall null effect of intravenous phosphate supplementation obscures a clinically important time-dependent pattern—an early protective signal followed by delayed harm—that precludes a simple risk-benefit assessment. This temporal heterogeneity, combined with a severity-dependent dose-response pattern showing protection concentrated in patients with phosphate <0.50 mmol/L, may help explain the contradictory findings in prior observational studies. These findings do not support routine supplementation for all ICU patients with mild-to-moderate hypophosphatemia. If supplementation is considered, it should be restricted to patients with severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L), pending confirmation in randomized trials.

**Keywords**: hypophosphatemia; intravenous phosphate; target trial emulation; SEQTaRget; 28-day mortality; intensive care; sequential trials; DAG; E-value; safety signals

---

## Introduction

Hypophosphatemia is one of the most common electrolyte disturbances in the intensive care unit, affecting approximately one in four critically ill patients [1]. Its pathophysiological consequences have been described in experimental and physiological studies: intracellular ATP depletion impairs myocardial contractility, diaphragmatic function, and immune competence [2,3]; reduced erythrocyte 2,3-diphosphoglycerate compromises tissue oxygen delivery [4]; and respiratory muscle dysfunction prolongs the duration of mechanical ventilation [3,5]. Taken together, these mechanisms offer a physiological rationale for phosphate repletion in the ICU.

Whether intravenous phosphate supplementation reduces mortality, however, is uncertain. Observational studies have yielded inconsistent findings: some reported protective effects [6], whereas others found no significant benefit [32,33,34]. Confounding by indication, whereby sicker patients more often receive phosphate therapy, obscures causal interpretation. Recent work suggests that hypophosphatemia may reflect disease severity rather than represent an independent risk factor [6,20]. The international GUTPHOS study is prospectively collecting phosphate disorder data [7]; however, adequately powered randomized evidence is absent and may be infeasible given the clinical equipoise surrounding this common ICU condition.

In the absence of randomized trials, target trial emulation offers a framework for causal inference from observational data [8,12,28,29,30,31]. The cloning-censoring-weighting (CCW) framework is designed to address two threats that have biased prior phosphate studies: immortal time bias and informative censoring. It emulates a hypothetical randomized trial by cloning each eligible patient into two identical records representing the treatment and control strategies, artificially censoring clones when they deviate from their assigned strategy, and applying inverse probability weighting to account for informative censoring [9,10,11,30]. The SEQTaRget R package [17] offers a standardized implementation of the CCW framework tailored for sequential trial designs. This approach is well suited for evaluating ICU interventions whose timing, dosing, and clinical context are dynamic, precisely the circumstances under which conventional observational methods are most vulnerable to immortal time bias and confounding by indication.

The present study extends the phosphate supplementation literature in four ways. First, it applies the standardized SEQTaRget CCW framework—for the first time to this clinical question—with DAG-driven covariate selection (14 confounders). Second, it characterizes time-dependent treatment effects using daily-resolution hazard ratios, revealing a temporal pattern that a single summary measure would obscure. Third, it identifies effect modifiers through interaction testing with FDR correction. Fourth, it transparently reports proportional hazards assumption violations and substantive limitations, establishing an evidentiary standard for future pharmacoepidemiology studies of time-dependent ICU interventions.

## Methods

### Study Design and Data Source

We employed a sequential enrollment target trial emulation design. The derivation cohort was drawn from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV v3.1) [13], covering ICU admissions at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Boston, Massachusetts) from 2008 through 2022. The external validation cohort used the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD v2.0) [14], comprising multi-center ICU data from across the United States (2014–2015). Data were accessed through PhysioNet credentialed access. The MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD databases contain de-identified patient data; the institutional review boards at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (MIMIC-IV) and the respective eICU-CRD contributing sites waived the requirement for informed consent. This study was exempted from additional institutional review board review. This study adheres to the TARGET 2025 reporting guideline [15]; the complete TARGET checklist is provided in Supplementary Table S1.

### Causal Assumptions

Three core assumptions underpin the validity of this target trial emulation. **Consistency**: the observed outcome under the assigned treatment strategy equals the counterfactual outcome. Because IV phosphate regimens vary in dose, formulation, and duration, this assumption may be partially violated, but our ITT estimand targets the treatment strategy (any IV phosphate vs. conservative management) rather than a specific dose. **Exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding)**: the DAG14 covariate set is sufficient to achieve conditional exchangeability between treatment groups. The primary analysis E-value was 1.04 (E-value near 1.0 for a null result indicates that an unmeasured confounder of any strength could explain the result as null). The Day 1 protective signal had an E-value of 3.23 (95% CI, 2.02), indicating that this time-specific effect remains stable against higher unmeasured confounding strength, as reported here. **Positivity**: all patients have a non-zero probability of receiving either treatment strategy. SEQTaRget's diagnostic assessment confirmed that 5 of 6 meta-analysis periods satisfied the positivity assumption. IPTW-weighted covariate balance was adequate (all post-weighting SMD <0.1; Supplementary Table S3).

### Emulation of the Target Trial

**Table 1. Target Trial Protocol and Observational Emulation**

| Component | Hypothetical Trial | Observational Emulation | Deviation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Eligibility criteria** | Age ≥18; ICU stay ≥24h; serum phosphate ≤0.80 mmol/L; no ESRD/chronic dialysis | Same criteria applied to EHR data | None |
| **Treatment strategies** | IV phosphate supplementation vs. conservative management | Identified from medication administration records | Non-blinded; dose and formulation at clinician discretion |
| **Grace period** | 12 hours from time zero for supplementation initiation | Same | None |
| **Washout between enrollments** | 48 hours minimum between sequential enrollments | Same | None |
| **Assignment procedures** | Randomized allocation | Observational assignment; DAG-driven confounder adjustment (14 variables) | Non-randomized; indication confounding present |
| **Time zero** | Time of qualifying phosphate measurement | Same | None |
| **Follow-up** | 28 days from enrollment | Same; censored at ICU discharge or 28 days | Death after ICU discharge may be incompletely captured |
| **Outcome** | 28-day all-cause mortality | Ascertained from EHR death records | None |
| **Causal estimand** | Intention-to-treat effect | SEQTaRget ITT with Rubin's rules (m=20) | Observational ITT ≠ randomized ITT |

The 48-hour washout period was selected based on the pharmacokinetics of intravenous phosphate: the serum phosphate half-life following IV administration is approximately 4–6 hours in critically ill patients [3], making 48 hours (>8 half-lives) sufficient to ensure that phosphate levels from a prior supplementation episode have returned to baseline before a new enrollment. This 48-hour window is consistent with standard practice in sequential trial emulations of time-varying ICU interventions [8,12] and provides a conservative buffer against potential carryover effects from prior supplementation episodes.
The 12-hour grace period was selected to balance clinical realism with treatment strategy contrast. In ICU practice, this window from the qualifying phosphate measurement allows sufficient time for result review, clinical assessment, phosphate ordering, pharmacy dispensing, and intravenous administration. This duration is consistent with previous target trial emulations of time-varying ICU interventions [8,12] and ensures that the intention-to-treat estimand reflects the effect of assigning to a supplementation strategy rather than the effect of immediate administration—which would not reflect real-world clinical practice. A sensitivity analysis using a 24-hour grace period (SA6) tested the robustness of this assumption.

### Sequential Enrollment Strategy

Patients could enroll multiple times during their ICU stay when meeting the following criteria: each new episode of hypophosphatemia (serum phosphate ≤0.80 mmol/L) with a minimum 48-hour washout period between enrollments and a maximum of 8 enrollments per patient. Screening was performed every 24 hours. A sensitivity analysis restricted to first enrollment assessed the impact of repeated enrollments on the effect estimate.

### DAG-Driven Covariate Selection


Fourteen core confounders were identified as the minimally sufficient adjustment set through directed acyclic graph (DAG) analysis. This selection was informed by the hypophosphatemia pathophysiological literature [6,20,25] and systematic assessment of variable availability in the MIMIC-IV database, following established guidance for confounding control in causal inference studies [39]. Variable selection followed three principles: each variable must be a common cause of both treatment assignment and outcome; mediators and post-treatment variables were excluded; and highly collinear variable pairs were avoided. The original DAG12 set (V26.8) was expanded to DAG14 by adding corrected calcium (corrected_calcium_mmol_min) because calcium-phosphate homeostasis is jointly regulated by parathyroid hormone and renal function, making calcium a shared driver of both treatment decisions and outcomes [21,22]; and nutrition support type (nutrition_support_type) because enteral and parenteral nutrition are major determinants of phosphate supplementation practice and independently influence mortality through nutritional pathways [23].

To empirically validate the DAG-driven selection, we performed a data-driven variable screening using multiple-imputation treatment-selection LASSO (MITS-LASSO) across all available candidate covariates. Of the 14 DAG-specified confounders, 11 (78.6%) were independently selected by LASSO at the ≥50% sensitivity threshold (C2) across 20 MICE-imputed datasets; at the more stringent ≥80% threshold (C1 primary threshold), 31 variables (including 11 DAG14 variables) were selected from 56 candidates. The three non-selected variables at the C2 threshold (admission_type, gender, and nutrition_support_type) had the lowest a priori causal relevance in the DAG framework. A complete-case SEQTaRget ITT analysis restricted to LASSO-selected covariates (n=8,566 complete cases, bootstrap=50) yielded a consistent null estimate (HR=0.978; 95% CI, 0.841–1.138; p=0.777; Supplementary Table S7), confirming that the DAG14-based primary result is not sensitive to the covariate selection approach. An additional sensitivity analysis using the V2pp (version 2 person-period) person-period framework with DAG14-forced plus LASSO-selected covariates (33 total) across 20 MICE imputations yielded a consistent null estimate (HR=0.946; 95% CI, 0.848–1.057; p=0.327), further confirming the robustness of the covariate selection strategy.

In the SEQTaRget CCW framework, categorical variables are processed through R's `model.matrix()`, which automatically creates dummy variables (treatment contrast, k−1 degrees of freedom for k-level factors). This encoding expands the 14 DAG14 variables to approximately 25–30 model terms, depending on the number of levels in each categorical variable.

### Missing Data Processing

Multiple imputation using chained equations (MICE) was used to handle missing data, with m=20 imputed datasets, maxit=20 iterations, and seed=12345 (all 20 imputations generated in a single MICE run), following established MICE methodology [35,36,37]. Predictive mean matching was used for continuous variables and logistic regression for binary variables. The outcome variable (28-day mortality) was included as a predictor in the imputation model but was not itself imputed (following Moons et al., 2006 [18]); the treatment variable was included as a predictor but was not imputed. Missingness rates for all DAG14 variables were below 5% except for lactate_t0 (31.3%): age 0%, gender 0%, baseline_sofa 0.3%, sepsis3 0%, charlson 0.1%, egfr 3.2%, invasive_vent_at_t0 0%, vasoactive_at_t0 0%, admission_type 0%, baseline_phosphate 0%, lactate_t0 31.3%, refeeding_risk 1.8%, corrected_calcium 4.8%, nutrition_support_type 0.2%. Convergence was confirmed through trace plots. MICE output was saved as Parquet files for each imputed dataset (v28_mice_imputed_imp01–20.parquet), containing imputed covariates and key identifiers (stay_id, trial_num) to ensure deterministic merging alignment. A complete-case analysis using DAG12 variables retained 96.8% of the cohort (31,891 of 32,330 trial-periods) and yielded results consistent with the MICE-based primary analysis.

### Primary Analysis: SEQTaRget ×20 with Rubin's Rules

The primary analysis was the SEQTaRget ITT analysis, applied independently to all 20 MICE imputed datasets, with results combined using Rubin's rules [19]. The IPTW-based analysis followed established methods for inverse probability weighting and marginal structural models [38,41,45]. Each imputation-specific analysis used the full sequential trial dataset (32,330 trial-periods) with 14 DAG-specified covariates and 200 bootstrap iterations. Cloning of the 32,330 trial-periods produced 64,660 cloned records per imputation. Censoring occurred at the time of strategy deviation (phosphate administration time for control clones, or the end of the phosphate-free interval for treatment clones); at 28 days, 82.6% of cloned records survived to the end of follow-up under the ITT estimand. The SEQTaRget framework implements the CCW method in five steps. First, each eligible patient-period is cloned into two identical records representing the treatment and control strategies. Second, artificial censoring occurs when a clone deviates from its assigned strategy. Third, the ITT estimand is estimated under the cloned data structure (without IPTW weighting). Fourth, a Cox proportional hazards model is fitted to the cloned data, with period-specific estimates summarized using a fixed-effects meta-analysis approach. Fifth, confidence interval estimation uses 200 bootstrap iterations, and the 20 imputation-specific log(HR) estimates are combined using Rubin's rules (W=0.00237 within-imputation variance; B=0.00025 between-imputation variance; total pooled SE=0.0513). The SEQTaRget `SEQuential()` function was called with parameters `method = "ITT"`, `bootstrap = TRUE`, `bootstrap.nboot = 200`, and `ncores = 1`; the DAG14 covariates were provided as fixed covariates. The 20 imputation-specific HR estimates ranged from 0.949 to 1.014 (SD=0.022), confirming stable imputation performance.

Because the global Schoenfeld test strongly rejected the proportional hazards assumption (see § Proportional Hazards Assessment), the ITT HR represents a time-averaged effect—a weighted average of the time-varying hazard ratio, weighted by the number of events at each time point. Under PH violation, this estimand does not have a direct causal interpretation as a constant 28-day hazard ratio. Therefore, we specified the RMST difference as a primary estimand and report piecewise HRs as complementary characterizations.


The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using Schoenfeld residuals. Because the global test was significant (p<0.0001), we also report the 28-day restricted mean survival time difference (as a primary estimand not dependent on the PH assumption), piecewise hazard ratios across pre-specified time intervals (0–3, 3–7, 7–14, 14–28 days), and daily-resolution hazard ratios for Days 1–14.

### Sensitivity Analyses

Thirteen pre-specified sensitivity analyses (SA1–SA13; Table 10) were organized across five dimensions of model and population variation. For model specification, we performed IPTW-Cox regression (Rubin's rules, m=5 imputed datasets) using inverse probability of treatment weights, and a Weibull accelerated failure time model (Rubin's rules) to estimate the survival time ratio. For causal estimand, the per-protocol CCW+IPTW analysis (SEQTaRget PP, bootstrap=50) estimated the complier average causal effect. For exposure definition, we stratified by phosphate administration route (oral [PO] vs. non-oral [IV or no supplementation]; PO: n=8,848; non-PO: n=23,445). Bootstrap stability was assessed by comparing bootstrap=200 vs. bootstrap=100 iterations. For population variation, the first-enrollment-only analysis restricted the cohort to each patient's first eligible enrollment (n=22,685 patients), and the eICU external validation (SEQTaRget ITT, bootstrap=100) used 11 shared covariates (sepsis3 was unavailable in eICU) covering 34,882 trial-periods. In response to reviewer concerns regarding sepsis3 data quality, we performed a DAG13 sensitivity analysis excluding sepsis3 from the DAG14 covariate set to assess its impact on the effect estimate. For model diagnostics, we conducted Schoenfeld residual tests, piecewise Cox models, and daily-resolution Cox models with cluster-robust standard errors. To assess the sensitivity of the primary analysis to the washout period definition, we performed a sensitivity analysis using a 24-hour washout window (SA14; SEQTaRget ITT, DAG14, MICE m=5, bootstrap=50), which yielded a consistent null estimate (HR=0.996; 95% CI, 0.876–1.132; p=0.952).

Two additional post-hoc sensitivity analyses were performed. First, the treatment definition was expanded to any phosphate supplementation (IV or enteral) versus strict conservative management (no phosphate within 12 hours), analyzed using the SEQTaRget ITT framework across all sequential trial-periods (full period, Rubin m=5, bootstrap=50, DAG14 covariates). The clinical motivation for this analysis was to test whether any form of phosphate supplementation—regardless of administration route—alters mortality, but it must be interpreted cautiously because the expanded treatment group merges the highest-risk (IV) and lowest-risk (enteral) patients, introducing inherent heterogeneity. Second, to explore the difference between the SEQTaRget framework's standard risk estimation approach (g-computation incorporating DAG14 covariates into the outcome prediction GLM) and conventional IPTW-Cox regression (direct adjustment for DAG14 covariates in the Cox model), we performed a head-to-head method comparison restricted to first enrollment (trial period 1) for IV vs. conservative management, using DAG14 covariates (SEQTaRget: bootstrap=50; IPTW-Cox: stabilized IPTW weights, truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles).

### Analysis Hierarchy and Multiplicity Control

All analyses were classified into four pre-specified tiers:

| Tier | Category | Examples | Multiplicity Control |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Primary** | Confirmatory | ITT HR (28-day), RMST difference | α = 0.05 (complementary, two tests) |
| **Secondary** | Pre-specified | 4 outcome domains, piecewise HRs | Bonferroni (α=0.0125) |
| **Exploratory** | Hypothesis-generating | 18 subgroups, 10 interactions, 14 daily HRs, 16 sensitivity analyses | FDR (q<0.10, interactions only); remainder descriptive |
| **Post-hoc** | Post-hoc | SA14 (any supplementation), SA15 (SEQTaRget vs IPTW-Cox comparison) | Uncorrected; explicitly labeled |

Post-hoc analyses (SA14–SA15) were conducted after the primary results were known and are reported separately from pre-specified analyses.


We pre-specified a hierarchical multiplicity control framework encompassing approximately 69 hypothesis tests across four analytic tiers:

**Tier 1—Primary analysis** (1 primary + 1 complementary estimand): The primary estimand was the 28-day RMST difference, which does not depend on the PH assumption. The complementary estimand was the ITT HR, reported as a time-averaged effect because the PH assumption was strongly violated.

**Tier 2—Supplementary pre-specified estimands** (4 tests): Four pre-specified piecewise HRs (0–3, 3–7, 7–14, 14–28 days). These estimands serve as complements to the primary estimand under the PH violation framework; no individual significance is claimed.

**Tier 3—Secondary outcome domains** (4 domains): Bonferroni correction α = 0.05/4 = 0.0125. Phosphate normalization was excluded as a treatment process measure.

**Tier 4—Exploratory analyses** (approximately 59 tests): 18 subgroup analyses, 10 interaction tests, 14 daily-resolution HRs, 16 sensitivity analyses, and 3 cardiovascular subcomponents. These analyses are hypothesis-generating. For the 10 interaction tests, we report FDR-corrected q-values (Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, q<0.10) as secondary multiplicity control. All remaining exploratory estimates are reported with nominal 95% confidence intervals for descriptive purposes; individual p-values are not considered confirmatory evidence. Under a global Benjamini-Hochberg procedure across all Tier 4 tests, no exploratory finding would remain significant, and we explicitly emphasize this.

The Day 1 protective signal (HR=0.565, nominal p=0.001) is an exploratory observation; it remains significant after Bonferroni correction for 14 daily tests (α=0.0036) but would not survive global multiplicity correction across all 69 tests. We present it as hypothesis-generating evidence of time-dependent treatment effects, not as a confirmatory finding.

### Subgroup and Interaction Analyses

Eighteen pre-specified subgroup analyses were conducted using SEQTaRget ITT with cluster-robust standard errors (cluster=stay_id) and Rubin's rules across 20 imputed datasets: by phosphate level (<0.50 vs. ≥0.50 mmol/L), Sepsis-3 status, SOFA severity (<8 vs. ≥8), age (<65 vs. ≥65 years), sex, invasive ventilation, vasoactive agent use, renal function (eGFR <60 vs. ≥60), and refeeding risk. Ten multiplicative interaction tests were performed using Cox proportional hazards models with cluster-robust standard errors (cluster=stay_id), each including a treatment × variable interaction term with the full DAG14 covariate set, following the framework for interaction and effect modification analysis described by VanderWeele [40]. Continuous variables were mean-centered before constructing interaction terms. To control the false discovery rate across the 10 interaction tests, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (q<0.10 considered significant) [24]. Given the multiple testing burden, the interaction analyses are hypothesis-generating; we report both raw p-values and FDR q-values to allow readers to assess the evidence strength at various significance thresholds.

Prompted by the protective signal observed in the pre-specified phosphate <0.50 mmol/L subgroup, we conducted a post-hoc phosphate threshold dose-response analysis to identify the protective threshold boundary. Seven pre-specified phosphate cutoffs (0.32, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.80 mmol/L) were evaluated, each using the same SEQTaRget ITT framework with cluster-robust SE and m=20 Rubin's rules, excluding baseline_phosphate from the DAG14 covariate set (as an effect modifier, not a confounder). Additionally, a restricted cubic spline (RCS) interaction analysis with 4 knots at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles was performed to assess nonlinearity of the treatment × phosphate interaction. This post-hoc analysis is exploratory and hypothesis-generating; p-values are not corrected for multiplicity.

### Secondary Outcomes

Four pre-specified secondary outcome domains were analyzed using the SEQTaRget CCW framework (ITT estimand, DAG14 covariates, bootstrap=25, m=5, Rubin's rules combined): (1) mortality domain (ICU mortality, hospital mortality, 90-day all-cause mortality, sharing domain-level α); (2) cardiovascular composite outcome (3 components: myocardial injury, new arrhythmia, or cardiogenic shock); (3) AKI KDIGO stage ≥2; (4) transfusion requirement. The SEQTaRget CCW framework was chosen for consistency with the primary analysis and to address immortal time bias and informative censoring inherent in time-dependent treatment decisions. Three cardiovascular subcomponents (new arrhythmia, myocardial injury, vasopressor escalation) are reported descriptively, not included in the Bonferroni correction. The 2-component and composite cardiovascular outcomes are retained as supplementary sensitivity analyses. Continuous outcomes (VFD-28, ICU length of stay) were analyzed using IPTW-weighted linear regression. To control multiplicity across the four independent secondary outcome domains (phosphate normalization was excluded as a treatment process check), Bonferroni correction α = 0.05/4 = 0.0125 was applied. Logistic regression (DAG14 covariate adjustment) was performed as a sensitivity analysis to facilitate comparison with prior observational literature.

#### E-value Analysis

E-values were calculated using the formula of VanderWeele and Ding (2017) [16]. Because the outcome incidence (17.4%) exceeds the range within which the hazard ratio approximates the risk ratio (<10%), we applied an HR→OR transformation (OR ≈ HR × (1−p)/(1−p×HR)) before calculating E-values. Bootstrap confidence intervals for the E-value were obtained by computing E-values for each of the 200 bootstrap HR estimates and taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For the null primary estimate (HR=0.987), the E-value is interpreted as the confounding strength required to move the point estimate to a clinically meaningful protective threshold (HR=0.90), rather than to the null. For the Day 1 protective signal (HR=0.565), the E-value also quantifies the confounding strength required to explain away the observed protective association (3.23; 95% CI, 2.02).

#### Missing Data Mechanism Sensitivity (MNAR)

To assess the sensitivity of the primary analysis to departures from the missing-at-random (MAR) assumption underlying MICE imputation, we performed a delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Analysis S8). This method applies a systematic shift Δ (delta) to the log hazard ratio across all 20 imputed datasets, then re-applies Rubin's rules for pooling. The magnitude of Δ represents the assumed strength of the missing-not-at-random (MNAR) mechanism. At Δ = 0 (MAR), the pooled HR = 0.987 (95% CI, 0.893–1.092). The tipping point for a statistically significant protective effect (benefit) was Δ = −0.16 (corresponding to OR = 27.9 for the association between missing data and mortality in the treated group), and the tipping point for statistically significant harm was Δ = +0.06 (OR = 3.5; Supplementary Figure S8). Given the low covariate missingness rates (highest: corrected calcium at 4.8%), both tipping points represent clinically implausible strong MNAR mechanisms, confirming that the primary null conclusion is stable against plausible departures from the MAR assumption.

### Pre-registration

This study was not pre-registered in a public registry prior to data analysis, as is common for retrospective electronic health record database studies. However, a structured Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) was finalized before the initiation of analysis and is provided in Supplementary S10. The tiered analysis framework (Tiers 1–4) was specified in the SAP, including the pre-specified primary estimands, sensitivity analyses, subgroup definitions, and secondary outcome domains. All post-hoc analyses (SA14, SA15) are explicitly labeled as such in the manuscript. The study has been retrospectively registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF; registration: https://osf.io/yc6kb/). The Statistical Plan (SAP) is provided in Supplementary S10.

### Software and Reproducibility

All analyses were performed using R version 4.4 with the SEQTaRget package (Chauvet et al., 2024) [17]. Complete analysis code—including all SQL extraction scripts, R analysis pipelines, and figure generation code—has been publicly released at [GitHub repository URL, to be provided upon manuscript acceptance]. All random processes used fixed seeds: SEQTaRget bootstrap used seed = 20260629, and MICE used seed = 12345 (all 20 imputations generated in a single MICE run) to ensure reproducibility. Complete sessionInfo() output is provided in Supplementary Analysis S7.

## Results

### Study Population

The derivation cohort comprised 22,685 eligible patients contributing 32,330 sequential trial-periods (median 1 enrollment per patient, IQR 1–1; range 1–8), with 5,610 observed 28-day deaths (17.4%). The treatment group (IV phosphate) included 5,147 trial-periods (15.9%), and the control group included 27,183 trial-periods (84.1%). Patients who received IV phosphate had higher disease severity: higher baseline SOFA scores (SMD=0.237), higher prevalence of sepsis-3 (SMD=0.229), higher vasoactive agent use (SMD=0.214), and lower baseline phosphate levels (SMD=0.707), consistent with confounding by indication (Table 3; participant flow diagram shown in Figure 2).

### Primary Analysis and Sensitivity Analyses

**Primary results.** The SEQTaRget ITT analysis (Rubin's rules across 20 imputed datasets, bootstrap=200, DAG14 covariates) showed no significant association between intravenous phosphate supplementation and 28-day mortality (HR=0.987; 95% CI, 0.893–1.092; p=0.802; 5,610 events; Table 4). The IPTW-weighted Kaplan-Meier survival curves showed considerable overlap between treatment and control groups throughout the 28-day follow-up (Figure 4A), consistent with the null finding. The 20 imputation-specific HR estimates ranged from 0.949 to 1.014 (SD=0.022), confirming the stability of the MICE procedure. CCW diagnostic assessment confirmed adequate trial structure across 6 sequential meta-analysis periods.

**Sensitivity analyses.** All sensitivity analyses were consistent with the overall null finding (Table 4). The DAG13 sensitivity analysis (excluding sepsis3) yielded HR=0.969 (95% CI, 0.875–1.072), with a relative HR difference of 1.8% from the primary DAG14 estimate. IPTW-Cox regression (Rubin's rules) yielded HR=1.054 (95% CI, 0.975–1.141), Weibull AFT yielded a survival time ratio of 0.989 (95% CI, 0.940–1.041), first-enrollment-only analysis yielded HR=1.047 (95% CI, 0.951–1.154), and per-protocol CCW+IPTW analysis yielded HR=0.979 (95% CI, 0.885–1.083). Bootstrap stability was confirmed (HR difference <0.001 between 200 and 100 iterations). A complete-case SEQTaRget ITT analysis restricted to LASSO-selected covariates (n=8,566 complete cases, bootstrap=50) yielded a consistent null estimate (HR=0.978; 95% CI, 0.841–1.138; p=0.777; Supplementary Table S7). An analysis using the V2pp (version 2 person-period) person-period framework with DAG14-forced plus LASSO-selected covariates (33 total) across 20 MICE imputations yielded HR=0.946 (95% CI, 0.848–1.057; p=0.327; Table 4 V2pp DAG14+LASSO). The 24h grace period sensitivity analysis using SEQTaRget ITT (DAG14, m=5, boot=50) yielded HR=0.976 (95% CI, 0.893–1.065; p=0.582; Table 10 SA13). The 24-hour washout window sensitivity analysis (SA14) yielded a consistent null estimate (HR=0.996; 95% CI, 0.876–1.132; p=0.952), confirming that the primary result is stable against the choice of washout period.

Stratification by phosphate administration route (PO vs. non-PO) showed no significant effect in either subgroup (PO: HR=1.075; 95% CI, 0.873–1.325; non-PO: HR=1.053; 95% CI, 0.931–1.190; Table 4b, Figure S4). The conventional Cox model without CCW framework yielded a directionally opposite result (HR=0.899; 95% CI, 0.826–0.980; p=0.015), underscoring the importance of addressing immortal time bias. The eICU-CRD external validation confirmed the null finding (HR=1.087; 95% CI, 0.913–1.293). The E-value was close to 1.0 (point estimate E=1.04), and the MNAR delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis confirmed stability against plausible departures from the MAR assumption.

### Post-hoc Sensitivity Analyses

Two post-hoc sensitivity analyses provided additional insights. First, when the treatment definition was expanded to any phosphate supplementation (IV or enteral) versus strict conservative management, the SEQTaRget ITT analysis showed a protective association (HR=0.882; 95% CI, 0.818–0.951; Table 4, SA14). However, this result must be interpreted in the context of substantial indication confounding arising from treatment group heterogeneity. The three exposure groups (IV, oral/NG, conservative) showed a systematic severity gradient: oral/NG patients were least severe (mean SOFA=4.77; 28-day mortality=14.8%), conservative patients intermediate (SOFA=5.09; mortality=17.9%), and IV patients most severe (SOFA=6.10; mortality=20.3%). The PO versus non-PO stratification forest plot (Figure 6) further supports this interpretation: neither the oral phosphate subgroup (HR=1.075; 95% CI, 0.873–1.325) nor the non-PO subgroup (HR=1.053; 95% CI, 0.931–1.190) showed significant effects, while the protective signal in the "any supplementation" analysis (HR=0.882) arises entirely from combining oral and IV patients, a classic Simpson's paradox. This artifact illustrates the need to distinguishing administration routes when analyzing phosphate supplementation effects.

Second, the head-to-head method comparison between SEQTaRget and IPTW-Cox (IV-only, first enrollment, DAG14 covariates; Table 4, SA15) yielded directionally consistent protective estimates: SEQTaRget (g-computation, DAG14 in outcome GLM) produced HR=0.902, while IPTW-Cox (DAG14 directly in Cox model) produced HR=0.819 (95% CI, 0.766–0.874). This analysis is post-hoc and requires cautious interpretation given the first-enrollment restriction, reduced bootstrap iterations, and the aggregation of the biphasic temporal pattern into a single summary measure.

### Exploratory Dose-Response Analysis

An exploratory dose-response analysis was conducted among patients who received IV phosphate supplementation to examine whether cumulative IV phosphate dose was associated with 28-day mortality. Using conventional Cox regression (DAG14 covariates, cluster-robust standard errors), the cumulative IV phosphate dose showed no significant association with mortality (HR=1.001 per 10 mmol; 95% CI, 0.991–1.011; p=0.889; Supplementary Figure S13). Similarly, no significant difference was observed by phosphate formulation type (potassium phosphate vs. sodium phosphate; HR=1.026; 95% CI, 0.879–1.198; p=0.666; Supplementary Figure S14). These analyses are limited by conventional Cox regression rather than the CCW framework and should be interpreted as exploratory, as dose and formulation are post-randomization variables subject to confounding by indication.

### Effect Modification and Temporal Heterogeneity (Exploratory Analyses, Tier 4)

> All analyses in this section are exploratory (Tier 4) without global multiplicity correction. Significant findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

The global Schoenfeld residual test strongly rejected the proportional hazards assumption (p<0.0001; Figure S1). The 28-day RMST difference was −0.02 days (95% CI, −0.31 to 0.27; p=0.880), confirming no overall survival time benefit. As exploratory analyses triggered by the PH violation, daily-resolution HR analysis (Figure 7) revealed a temporal pattern: a protective effect on Day 1 (HR=0.565; 95% CI, 0.401–0.796; nominal p=0.001), followed by elevated risk during Days 5–8 (HR range 1.47–1.59, all nominal p<0.005), returning to null thereafter. The Day 1 protective signal remained significant after Bonferroni correction for 14 daily tests (α=0.0036). Piecewise Cox analysis confirmed this pattern (Figure 8), with the 3–7 day segment showing the strongest harmful effect (HR=1.308; 95% CI, 1.154–1.484; p<0.001), while the 0–3 day (HR=0.947), 7–14 day (HR=1.060), and 14–28 day (HR=0.981) segments showed no significant effects.

![Figure 7. Daily-Resolution Hazard Ratios (Days 1–14) — Cox regression with cluster-robust standard errors](../output/figures/Fig7_Daily_HR.png)

![Figure 8. Piecewise Hazard Ratios by Follow-up Interval — Four pre-specified time segments (0–3, 3–7, 7–14, 14–28 days)](../output/figures/Fig8_Piecewise_HR.png)

Subgroup analyses (Figure 5, Table 7) revealed a consistent protective trend across 18 pre-specified subgroups, with all point estimates below 1.0. The strongest protective signal was observed in patients with severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L: HR=0.803; 95% CI, 0.660–0.977; nominal p=0.029), which was the only subgroup reaching nominal statistical significance. Patients with moderate hypophosphatemia (phosphate ≥0.50 mmol/L) showed a null effect (HR=0.970; 95% CI, 0.883–1.065). The heterogeneity test between these two phosphate strata was borderline (Cochran's Q=2.87, p=0.090), suggesting a possible severity-dependent effect modification. All other subgroup comparisons showed non-significant protective trends, with no heterogeneity reaching statistical significance (all Q-test p>0.10).

#### Phosphate Threshold Dose-Response Analysis

Prompted by the protective signal in severe hypophosphatemia, we conducted a post-hoc threshold dose-response analysis to identify the protective threshold boundary (Table 7b, Figure S15). Across seven pre-specified phosphate thresholds (0.32, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, and 0.80 mmol/L), all point estimates remained below 1.0 (protective trend), with a clear dose-response pattern: the protective effect was strongest at the lowest thresholds and attenuated monotonically toward the null as the threshold increased. The protective effect reached nominal statistical significance only at the 0.50 mmol/L threshold (HR=0.806; 95% CI, 0.670–0.970; p=0.022; n=2,852; events=518), closely matching the pre-specified subgroup result (HR=0.803). A similar magnitude of protection was observed at the 0.40 mmol/L threshold (HR=0.802; 95% CI, 0.588–1.093; p=0.163; n=829; events=175), but did not reach significance due to limited sample size. At thresholds ≥0.60 mmol/L, the HR approached 1.0 (HR range 0.919–0.972; all p>0.10), indicating loss of protective effect. A restricted cubic spline interaction analysis (4 knots at 5%/35%/65%/95% percentiles; 0.45/0.65/0.71/0.78 mmol/L) did not detect a statistically significant treatment × phosphate nonlinear interaction (χ²=2.17, df=3, p=0.538), consistent with the discrete threshold analysis showing a gradual rather than abrupt transition. Collectively, these findings suggest that the protective effect of IV phosphate is concentrated in patients with baseline phosphate below 0.50 mmol/L, with the threshold at 0.50 mmol/L representing the boundary above which the benefit attenuates toward the null.

No interaction test reached the pre-specified FDR significance threshold (all q>0.10), consistent with the absence of strong effect modification.

### Secondary Outcomes

Four pre-specified secondary outcome domains were analyzed using the SEQTaRget CCW framework (ITT estimand, DAG14 covariates, bootstrap=25, m=5; Table 9). Two of the four domains reached statistical significance after Bonferroni correction (α=0.0125): transfusion requirement (HR=1.299; 95% CI, 1.181–1.428; p<0.001) and AKI KDIGO ≥2 (HR=1.115; 95% CI, 1.025–1.213; p=0.011). ## Discussion

In this target trial emulation of intravenous phosphate supplementation in critically ill adults with hypophosphatemia, the primary RMST estimand established no net survival benefit in the SEQTaRget CCW framework (RMST difference of −0.02 days (95% CI, −0.31 to 0.27; p=0.880), with the complementary time-averaged ITT HR of 0.987 (95% CI, 0.893–1.092; p=0.802). This null finding was consistent across DAG13 sensitivity (HR=0.969), IPTW-Cox (HR=1.054), Weibull AFT (STR=0.989), per-protocol (HR=0.979), and eICU external validation (HR=1.087). All 20 MICE datasets were combined via Rubin's rules (HR range 0.949–1.014; SD=0.022), enhancing confidence in this null result relative to single-imputation approaches. However, the proportional hazards assumption was strongly violated (Schoenfeld p<0.0001), indicating that a single summary HR inadequately characterizes the time-varying causal effect.

### Temporal Heterogeneity

The overall null effect arose from opposing effects across different time windows: early protection on Day 1 (HR=0.565; 95% CI, 0.401–0.796; E-value=3.23), followed by mid-term harm concentrated in the 3–7 day interval (HR=1.308; 95% CI, 1.154–1.484; p<0.001). The Day 1 protective signal remained significant after Bonferroni correction for 14 daily tests (α=0.0036) and was stable against moderate-to-strong unmeasured confounding (E-value=3.23). This protective signal was internally consistent with the protective trend observed across all 18 subgroups (all HR<1.0), with the strongest protective effect in severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L: HR=0.803; p=0.029), and was independently validated by the post-hoc SA15 method comparison.

### Relationship to Existing Literature

These findings are consistent with and extend prior work. Prior observational studies of phosphate supplementation in ICU patients have reported inconsistent conclusions [6], with recent evidence syntheses documenting significant between-study heterogeneity [6]. The observed protective trend across all severity strata, with the strongest protective signal in severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L), may help explain this heterogeneity: studies enriched for patients with severe hypophosphatemia would be expected to show more protective effects. This pattern is consistent with our subgroup findings.

This analysis extends prior work in several respects. By applying the CCW method through the SEQTaRget framework, we directly addressed immortal time bias that has compromised prior phosphate observational studies. Sensitivity analysis (SA10) demonstrated the magnitude of this issue: the conventional Cox model produced a statistically significant protective estimate (HR=0.899; p=0.015), directionally opposite to the CCW-corrected estimate (HR=0.987; p=0.802). This 9% relative difference reveals the source of inconsistency in the prior observational literature and underscores the importance of the CCW framework for time-dependent ICU exposures.

### Effect Modification

The temporal pattern was accompanied by a consistent protective trend across all subgroups, with effect modification strongest along the phosphate severity axis. None of the ten interaction tests reached the significance threshold after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (all q>0.10). The Charlson comorbidity index showed the only nominally significant interaction (HR=0.967 per unit; 95% CI, 0.942–0.993; p=0.013; q=0.134), with direction consistent with greater protection in more comorbid patients. Age showed a borderline interaction (p=0.082), suggesting a trend toward greater protection in younger patients. Subgroup analyses corroborated this protective pattern: all 18 subgroups showed point estimates below 1.0, with the strongest protective signal observed in severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L: HR=0.803; 95% CI, 0.660–0.977; nominal p=0.029). The heterogeneity test between the two phosphate strata was borderline (Cochran's Q=2.87, p=0.090), suggesting possible severity-dependent effect modification.

To further characterize the phosphate severity gradient, we conducted a post-hoc threshold dose-response analysis across seven phosphate cutoffs (0.32, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.80 mmol/L; Table 7b, Figure S15). The results revealed a monotonic dose-response pattern: the protective effect was strongest at the lowest thresholds (HR≈0.80 at both 0.40 and 0.50 mmol/L cutoffs), then attenuated progressively toward the null as the threshold increased (HR=0.92 at 0.60 mmol/L; HR=0.97 at 0.80 mmol/L, equivalent to the overall ITT HR=0.987). The protective effect reached nominal statistical significance only at the 0.50 mmol/L threshold (HR=0.806; 95% CI, 0.670–0.970; p=0.022), with the 0.40 mmol/L threshold showing similar effect magnitude but lacking power due to limited sample size (n=829). Notably, the restricted cubic spline interaction analysis did not detect a statistically significant nonlinear interaction (p=0.538), suggesting that the transition from protective to null effect is gradual rather than threshold-dependent. This dose-response pattern provides the strongest available evidence for a severity-based treatment indication: IV phosphate supplementation appears to confer a protective survival benefit only in patients with baseline phosphate below 0.50 mmol/L, with the effect attenuating monotonically above this level.

The biological plausibility of this gradient is compelling. In patients with severe hypophosphatemia, phosphorus depletion driven by increased metabolic demands from sepsis, tissue repair, and respiratory muscle work may create a true deficiency state amenable to supplementation. In patients with moderate hypophosphatemia, mild phosphate depletion may primarily reflect dilution, transcellular shifts, or transient reduced intake—states in which exogenous phosphate administration may not address the underlying physiology and could potentially cause harm through calcium-phosphate precipitation, hemodynamic effects, or iatrogenic fluid loading, particularly during the 3–7 day window.

Several mechanisms may explain the delayed harm signal observed during Days 3–7. First, calcium-phosphate product elevation following IV phosphate administration can lead to microvascular precipitation, particularly in patients with pre-existing renal impairment or hypercalcemia, potentially contributing to AKI and cardiovascular events [22]. Second, IV phosphate solutions are typically formulated as sodium or phosphate salts, introducing a substantial sodium load (approximately 20 mmol sodium per 10 mmol phosphate as sodium phosphate) that may exacerbate fluid overload and hemodynamic instability in vulnerable patients. Third, rapid correction of hypophosphatemia may trigger hypocalcemia through calcium-phosphate chelation, potentially contributing to arrhythmias and myocardial dysfunction [21]. Fourth, phosphate-induced intracellular shifts of and magnesium may destabilize cardiac membrane potentials and contribute to the observed arrhythmia signal. These mechanisms are consistent with the coherent pattern of safety signals observed across the cardiovascular, renal, and hematologic domains.


### Safety Signals

Collectively, temporal heterogeneity provides a unifying framework for interpreting the safety signals observed across multiple analytic domains. The 3–7 day piecewise HR showed a statistically significant 31% increase in mortality risk (HR=1.308; 95% CI, 1.154–1.484; p<0.001), and daily-resolution analysis confirmed significant harm during Days 5–8 (HR≥1.47). Using the SEQTaRget CCW framework, two of four secondary outcome domains showed significant effects after Bonferroni correction: a 30% increased transfusion requirement (HR=1.299; 95% CI, 1.181–1.428; p<0.001) and a 12% increased AKI KDIGO ≥2 (HR=1.115; 95% CI, 1.025–1.213; p=0.011). While the overall 28-day mortality point estimate was null (HR=0.987), the consistent protective trend across all 18 subgroups (all HR<1.0), the nominally significant protective effect in severe hypophosphatemia (phosphate <0.50 mmol/L: HR=0.803; p=0.029), and the post-hoc threshold analysis showing a monotonic dose-response pattern with HR=0.806 at the 0.50 mmol/L cutoff (p=0.022) collectively suggest that the delayed harm signal may partially offset an underlying protective effect, particularly in patients with severe physiological derangement.

### Strengths

This analysis has several methodological strengths. First, we used the SEQTaRget framework, a validated open-source R implementation of the CCW method. Its standardized cloning, censoring, and ITT estimation pipeline reduces analytic degrees of freedom that may arise in custom-coded CCW analyses. Second, the DAG-driven covariate selection process (14 variables, expanded from DAG12 to DAG14 by adding corrected calcium and nutrition support type) was based on a systematic review of the hypophosphatemia pathophysiological literature rather than purely data-driven selection. Third, applying Rubin's rules across all 20 MICE imputed datasets, rather than selecting a single imputation or averaging only point estimates, provides valid inference that fully accounts for imputation uncertainty. Fourth, we used multiple complementary time-to-event methods (RMST, which is not dependent on PH; piecewise HRs across four pre-specified intervals; and daily-resolution HRs), providing a more nuanced characterization of the treatment effect than a single Cox summary measure. Fifth, external validation in the eICU-CRD database, a multi-center cohort geographically and temporally distinct from MIMIC-IV, represents a meaningful step toward assessing transportability.

### Limitations

These strengths must be weighed against several limitations that affect the interpretation and generalizability of our findings.

**Unmeasured and residual confounding.** As with all observational studies, unmeasured confounding remains the most important threat to causal interpretation. Although our DAG14 set was selected through systematic literature review, with robustness confirmed by DAG13 sensitivity analysis, residual confounding from clinician preference, patient frailty, detailed nutritional status beyond the binary refeeding risk marker, and genetic factors affecting phosphorus metabolism may bias estimates. The E-value for the primary analysis point estimate approximates 1.0, indicating high sensitivity to unmeasured confounding and underscoring the inherent uncertainty of observational estimates even after rigorous adjustment.

**Competing risks.** Discharge alive from the ICU is a competing event for ICU mortality and could affect secondary outcome estimates. For the primary 28-day mortality outcome, competing risks are not a concern because 28-day mortality is a non-competing endpoint. For secondary outcomes (ICU and hospital mortality), we used the SEQTaRget CCW framework, which treats discharge as an administrative censoring event. This approach is standard in TTE analyses, but we acknowledge that cause-specific hazard or Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models would provide complementary estimates for outcomes where competing risks are relevant. Fine-Gray model results are provided in Supplementary S11 for the key secondary outcomes.

**Proportional hazards violation.** The global Schoenfeld test strongly rejected the PH assumption (p<0.0001). The time-averaged SEQTaRget ITT HR (0.987) therefore represents a weighted average of the time-varying effect weighted by the event-time distribution and should not be interpreted as a constant hazard ratio. We specified RMST as the primary estimand precisely because it is not dependent on the PH assumption.

**Day 1 protective signal interpretation.** The Day 1 protective signal (HR=0.565) should be interpreted with caution beyond multiplicity considerations. The timing of this effect—on the first day after enrollment—raises the possibility that it may partially reflect residual confounding rather than a true treatment effect. Patients who receive IV phosphate within the first hours of meeting eligibility criteria may differ from those who do not in ways not fully captured by the DAG14 covariate set, including unmeasured aspects of clinician judgment, rapidity of clinical deterioration, or the acuity of the underlying condition. Furthermore, the Day 1 effect could reflect immortal time bias if the outcome assessment window is not perfectly aligned with the time-zero definition. The E-value of 3.23 provides some protection against unmeasured confounding, but should be interpreted as an upper bound on the confounding strength required to explain the observed association, not as proof of a causal effect.

**Multiplicity.** Approximately 69 hypothesis tests were conducted across four analytic tiers. Only the primary hypothesis (Tier 1) and four secondary outcome domains (Tier 3) were protected by pre-specified multiplicity correction. Under a global Benjamini-Hochberg procedure across all Tier 4 tests (~59 comparisons), no exploratory finding, including nominally significant interactions and the Day 1 protective signal, would remain statistically significant. All Tier 4 results are therefore hypothesis-generating and require independent replication.

**Treatment definition and dose-response.** The ITT treatment definition aggregates heterogeneous dosing regimens. Our exploratory dose-response analysis (Supplementary Analysis S13) found no significant relationship between cumulative IV phosphate dose and 28-day mortality (HR=1.001 per 10 mmol; 95% CI, 0.991–1.011; p=0.889). No significant difference was observed by drug type (HR=1.026; p=0.666; Supplementary Analysis S14). However, these analyses used conventional Cox regression rather than the CCW framework and should be considered exploratory.

**Pre-registration.** This study was not pre-registered in a public registry. Although the Statistical Analysis Plan was finalized before analysis initiation, the ChiCTR registration was completed retrospectively after data analysis. The distinction between pre-specified and post-hoc analyses was documented in the SAP before results were examined, and all post-hoc analyses (SA14, SA15) are explicitly labeled. The tiered framework (Tiers 1–4) and all pre-specified analyses were documented in the SAP before results were examined.

**Post-hoc analysis interpretation.** The expanded exposure definition analysis (SA14) and the SEQTaRget vs. IPTW-Cox DAG14 method comparison (SA15) are both post-hoc. SA14: systematic bias assessment identified three concerns: (i) confounding by indication from merging lowest- and highest-risk patients into a single "any supplementation" treatment group; (ii) treatment group heterogeneity, as IV and enteral routes differ mechanistically; and (iii) the DAG14 covariate set may not adequately control for confounding in the enteral phosphate decision pathway. SA15: first-enrollment protective estimates require cautious interpretation under three important caveats: (i) the first-enrollment population is enriched for higher-acuity patients, producing a different treatment-effect profile than the multi-enrollment primary analysis population; (ii) reduced bootstrap iterations (boot=50 vs. boot=200) produce wider confidence intervals; and (iii) concordance with the pre-specified Day 1 protective signal (HR=0.565) supports biologic plausibility of early benefit, but the attenuated effect size (HR 0.819–0.902) reflects aggregation of the biphasic temporal pattern across all follow-up days.

### Evidence Certainty

Applying the GRADE framework, the certainty of evidence for the primary null finding is rated as **low** (Table S8). Observational evidence default to low certainty, and no criteria for upgrading were met: the effect size is close to the null (no large effect), no dose-response gradient was observed, and residual confounding from indication bias would likely bias against treatment benefit rather than toward it. The consistency of the null finding across eight sensitivity analyses, one external validation, and two analytic frameworks (SEQTaRget and V2pp) provides some reassurance against spurious findings, but does not elevate the evidence above low certainty. The exploratory safety signals (transfusion requirement, AKI KDIGO ≥2) and time-dependent effects (Day 1 protection, Days 3–7 harm) should be interpreted with appropriate caution given their post-hoc nature and the absence of global multiplicity correction.

### Clinical Implications

These findings carry implications for ICU practice. **First**, the overall null result for 28-day mortality does not support routine intravenous phosphate supplementation for all ICU patients with mild-to-moderate hypophosphatemia. Given that 84.1% of trial-periods received conservative management at the population level without apparent harm, the onus lies on those advocating universal supplementation.

**Second**, the consistent safety signals across multiple analytic domains (increased transfusion requirement, HR=1.299; AKI KDIGO ≥2, HR=1.115; new arrhythmia, HR=1.270; and vasopressor escalation, HR=1.182) constitute a coherent pattern warranting clinical caution, particularly in patients with underlying cardiovascular or renal disease.

**Third**, the post-hoc phosphate threshold dose-response analysis (Table 7b, Figure S15) provides the most actionable clinical insight: IV phosphate supplementation demonstrates a monotonic protective dose-response pattern, with the protective effect concentrated in patients with baseline phosphate below 0.50 mmol/L (HR=0.806; 95% CI, 0.670–0.970; p=0.022). A similar magnitude of protection was observed at the 0.40 mmol/L threshold (HR=0.802) but did not reach significance due to limited sample size. At thresholds ≥0.60 mmol/L, the HR attenuated progressively toward the null (HR=0.92–0.97). Combined with the borderline heterogeneity between phosphate strata (Cochran's Q=2.87, p=0.090), these findings suggest that if supplementation is considered, it should be prioritized for patients with baseline phosphate <0.50 mmol/L. The 0.50 mmol/L threshold represents a clinically meaningful boundary: below this level, the absolute 28-day mortality was 18.1% (518/2,852) in the analysis population, with a 19.4% relative risk reduction (HR=0.806); above this level, no survival benefit was observed.

**Fourth**, the three-phase temporal pattern has implications for clinical monitoring. Patients receiving IV phosphate should be monitored closely during the 3–7 day post-administration window, with particular attention to cardiovascular status, renal function, and transfusion requirements.

### Future Research Directions

Our findings identify several priority directions for future research. First, the protective dose-response pattern identified in the threshold analysis (Table 7b, Figure S15) and the time-dependent harm pattern provide a strong rationale for randomized controlled trials. Such trials should: (a) enrich for severe hypophosphatemia using the 0.50 mmol/L threshold as the primary enrollment criterion, with pre-specified subgroup analyses at 0.40 mmol/L to capture the most severely depleted patients; (b) incorporate systematic cardiovascular safety monitoring during the 3–7 day post-administration window; (c) pre-specify time-segment analyses as secondary endpoints (0–3, 3–7, 7–14, 14–28 days); (d) collect granular dosing data for dose-response characterization; and (e) use the 0.50 mmol/L threshold as a pre-specified effect modification variable to confirm the severity-based treatment indication suggested by our observational data.

Second, the contrast between the conventional Cox regression (HR=0.899, p=0.015) and the CCW analysis (HR=0.987, p=0.802) demonstrates that immortal time bias is a quantitatively important source of error in ICU pharmacoepidemiology. Future observational studies of time-dependent ICU interventions should adopt the CCW framework as standard analytic practice, consistent with the TARGET 2025 guideline recommendations.
